hints: Focus on whether each reaction can make only 2-chloropropane cleanly, or whether it makes a mixture or a different main product.
Remember that free radical chlorination of propane attacks both primary and secondary positions, while dilute aqueous reagents let water compete as a nucleophile.
Think about which reagent turns the poor -OH leaving group into a very good one and drives the reaction to completion by releasing gases.
walkthrough:
**Define the goal**

We want to make $\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_3$ specifically and in high yield. That means we need a selective reaction with no competing isomers or competing products.

Target:
$$\text{propan-2-ol or propene or propane} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_3$$

**Check the non-selective and unreactive routes**

Free radical substitution of propane gives both 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane, so the yield of the 2-isomer is poor. Dilute $\text{NaCl(aq)}$ cannot replace -OH because $\text{OH}^-$ is a poor leaving group and $\text{Cl}^-$ is a weak nucleophile in water.

**Compare the two addition or substitution routes**

Propene with concentrated $\text{HCl}$ would give 2-chloropropane by Markovnikov addition, but dilute aqueous $\text{HCl}$ means water competes and the major product is propan-2-ol. Propan-2-ol with $\text{SOCl}_2$ replaces -OH by -Cl cleanly in one step.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3 + \text{SOCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_3 + \text{SO}_2 + \text{HCl}$$

**Conclude the best yield**

Because $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{HCl}$ are gases that escape, the equilibrium is pulled to the right and no isomer mixture forms. This gives pure 2-chloropropane in the best yield.

options.A: Free radical substitution by UV light is not selective. Chlorine radicals can abstract a primary H to give 1-chloropropane or a secondary H to give 2-chloropropane, plus further substitution products, so the yield of pure 2-chloropropane is low.
options.B: No useful reaction occurs. The -OH group in an alcohol is a very poor leaving group, and dilute $\text{Cl}^-$ from NaCl is not acidic or powerful enough to replace it. Students choosing this confuse a source of chloride ions with a chlorinating agent.
options.C: This is the standard clean method to make a chloroalkane from an alcohol. $\text{SOCl}_2$ converts -OH into a good leaving group and delivers Cl, giving only $\text{CH}_3\text{CHClCH}_3$ with gaseous $\text{SO}_2$ and HCl by-products that escape and give a very high yield.
options.D: Electrophilic addition of HCl to propene could give 2-chloropropane by Markovnikov rule, but dilute aqueous acid means water is present in large excess. Water acts as the nucleophile instead of $\text{Cl}^-$, so the major product is propan-2-ol, not 2-chloropropane.
